4.text: The Henderson–Hasselbalch equation for the bicarbonate buffer

The concentration of H~2~CO~3~ in blood is hard to measure directly, so the partial pressure of CO~2~ is used instead (0.03 is the solubility coefficient of CO~2~ in plasma, mmol/L per mm Hg): pH = 6.1 + lg([HCO~3~^−^] / (0.03·pCO~2~)). Normally pH = 6.1 + lg(24 / 1.2) = 6.1 + lg20 = 7.4. The equation shows that pH depends on the ratio of HCO~3~^−^, **controlled by the kidneys**, to pCO~2~, **controlled by the lungs**.

**Chloride shift (Hamburger phenomenon).** In the tissues CO~2~ enters the red blood cell and is converted into H~2~CO~3~ by carbonic anhydrase; it dissociates into H^+^ (bound by hemoglobin) and HCO~3~^−^. HCO~3~^−^ leaves for the plasma, and Cl^−^ enters the red cell in its place to keep electroneutrality. In the lungs the process runs in reverse. Thanks to this, most CO~2~ is carried in the blood as HCO~3~^−^.

5.text: Anion gap and assessment of compensation

The sums of cations and anions in plasma are equal. The usually unmeasured anions (proteins, phosphates, sulfates, organic acids) are assessed by the **anion gap**: AG = [Na^+^] − ([Cl^−^] + [HCO~3~^−^]), normal **8–12 mmol/L**. It is the key indicator for dividing metabolic acidosis into two groups:

Mechanism
Causes

HCO~3~^−^ is lost and replaced by Cl^−^
diarrhea, intestinal fistulas, renal tubular acidosis

5.text: In metabolic acidosis the adequacy of respiratory compensation is checked with **Winter’s formula**: expected pCO~2~ = 1.5·[HCO~3~^−^] + 8 ± 2 (mm Hg). If the measured pCO~2~ is higher, there is an additional respiratory acidosis (for example, the patient is tiring and breathing is weakening); if it is lower — an additional respiratory alkalosis.

parts.text: Compensation never fully eliminates a disorder and **never pushes pH to the opposite side**. If pH is normal but pCO~2~ and HCO~3~^−^ are both markedly changed, it is usually a **mixed** disorder.

In alkalosis albumin loses H^+^ and binds more Ca^2+^ — **ionized calcium falls**. That is why during hyperventilation there is numbness around the lips and spasm of the fingers (“obstetrician’s hand”), even though total calcium is normal.

7.text: **Ammoniagenesis.** In the cells of the renal tubules glutamine is broken down to form NH~3~. NH~3~ passes into the tubular lumen, takes up H^+^ and is excreted in the urine as NH~4~^+^; for every H^+^ excreted, one new HCO~3~^−^ returns to the blood. In chronic acidosis ammoniagenesis increases several-fold — this is the main route of renal compensation.

insert.title: 0. Theories of acids and bases. Protolytic equilibrium

blocks.text: **Arrhenius theory:** an acid forms H^+^ in water, a base forms OH^−^. This theory cannot explain non-aqueous media or bases such as NH~3~. According to the **Brønsted–Lowry protolytic theory**, **an acid is a proton donor** and **a base is a proton acceptor**. After an acid gives up a proton, its **conjugate base** remains: CH~3~COOH / CH~3~COO^−^, NH~4~^+^ / NH~3~, H~2~CO~3~ / HCO~3~^−^. **Lewis theory** defines an acid as an electron-pair acceptor (Fe^3+^, BF~3~) — the chemistry of complexes is based on it.

The dissociation of a weak acid is expressed by the **acidity constant**: K~a~ = [H^+^]·[A^−^] / [HA], pK~a~ = −lgK~a~. The smaller the pK~a~, the stronger the acid. For a conjugate pair K~a~·K~b~ = K~w~, that is, pK~a~ + pK~b~ = 14. **Ostwald’s dilution law:** the degree of dissociation of a weak electrolyte α ≈ √(K / C) — α increases when the solution is diluted.

blocks.text: **Hydrolysis of salts.** A solution of a salt of a weak acid and a strong base is alkaline (NaHCO~3~ solution pH ≈ 8.3, CH~3~COONa), and a salt of a strong acid and a weak base is acidic (NH~4~Cl). That is why sodium hydrogen carbonate is used as an antacid and a urine-alkalinizing agent, and ammonium chloride as a urine-acidifying agent.

parts.text: Most drugs are weak acids or bases. Only the **un-ionized** form crosses membranes well. The ratio of the ionized and un-ionized forms is found from the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation: for an acid lg([A^−^] / [HA]) = pH − pK~a~. For example, acetylsalicylic acid (pK~a~ ≈ 3.5) is mostly un-ionized in the acidic stomach and is partly absorbed there.

skills.title: Skill: analyzing metabolic acidosis by the anion gap

items: Confirm that pH < 7.35 and HCO~3~^−^ < 22 mmol/L — this is metabolic acidosis.
Calculate the anion gap: AG = Na^+^ − (Cl^−^ + HCO~3~^−^); normal 8–12 mmol/L.
If the AG is increased, look for organic acids: glucose and ketones, lactate, creatinine, a history of poisoning.
If the AG is normal, look for loss of HCO~3~^−^: diarrhea, renal tubular disease.
Check respiratory compensation with Winter’s formula: expected pCO~2~ = 1.5·HCO~3~^−^ + 8 ± 2.

cases.title: Problem 4
cases.text: A patient who drank a technical liquid instead of alcohol has blurred vision and deep, rapid breathing. Tests: pH 7.15; Na^+^ 140, Cl^−^ 100, HCO~3~^−^ 10 mmol/L; pCO~2~ 23 mm Hg.
cases.ask: Determine the type of acid–base disorder, calculate the anion gap and assess the respiratory compensation. What is the likely cause?
cases.answer: pH and HCO~3~^−^ are low — **metabolic acidosis**. AG = 140 − (100 + 10) = **30 mmol/L** — sharply increased; an organic acid has been added to the blood. Winter’s formula: expected pCO~2~ = 1.5 · 10 + 8 = 23 ± 2 — equal to the measured 23, so respiratory compensation is adequate (Kussmaul breathing). Together with the visual disturbance this is typical of **methanol** poisoning: methanol is converted in the liver into formic acid, which damages the optic nerve. Treatment: fomepizole or ethanol (stops the oxidation of methanol), NaHCO~3~, hemodialysis.

cases.title: Problem 5
cases.text: A child swallowed a large number of acetylsalicylic acid tablets. The pK~a~ of salicylic acid is ≈ 3.
cases.ask: Calculate the ratio of ionized to un-ionized salicylate at urine pH 5 and 8. Why is the urine alkalinized in treatment?
cases.answer: lg([A^−^] / [HA]) = pH − pK~a~. At pH 5: 5 − 3 = 2, ratio 10^2^ = **100 : 1**; at pH 8: 8 − 3 = 5, ratio 10^5^ = **100 000 : 1**. In alkaline urine the un-ionized (membrane-permeable) form is 1000 times smaller — salicylate is not reabsorbed in the tubules, is **“trapped”** in the urine and excreted quickly. That is why NaHCO~3~ is given to keep the urine pH at 7.5–8.5.

cases.title: Problem 6
cases.text: A student who is very anxious before an exam is breathing rapidly; there is numbness around the lips and the fingers are cramping. Blood gases: pH 7.52; pCO~2~ 28 mm Hg; HCO~3~^−^ 22 mmol/L.
cases.ask: What is the disorder? Why did the cramps appear? What help is given?
cases.answer: pH is raised, pCO~2~ is lowered and HCO~3~^−^ is still normal — **acute respiratory alkalosis** (hyperventilation; renal compensation has not yet started). In alkalosis albumin binds more Ca^2+^, **ionized calcium falls** and neuromuscular excitability increases — hence the paresthesia and cramps. Help: calm the person and slow their breathing; as CO~2~ is restored in the blood, the symptoms disappear.

cases.title: Problem 7
cases.text: A patient’s blood gases: HCO~3~^−^ 12 mmol/L, pCO~2~ 25 mm Hg.
cases.ask: Calculate the blood pH using the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation and assess the disorder.
cases.answer: pH = 6.1 + lg(12 / (0.03 · 25)) = 6.1 + lg(12 / 0.75) = 6.1 + lg16 = 6.1 + 1.2 = **7.3**. pH is low and HCO~3~^−^ is decreased — **metabolic acidosis**; the decreased pCO~2~ is respiratory compensation (expected pCO~2~ = 1.5 · 12 + 8 = 26 ± 2, measured 25 — compensation is adequate).

cases.title: Problem 8
cases.text: A long-term smoker with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Blood gases: pH 7.36; pCO~2~ 60 mm Hg; HCO~3~^−^ 33 mmol/L.
cases.ask: Identify the disorder and explain the compensation mechanism. Why is high-concentration oxygen given to such a patient with caution?
cases.answer: pCO~2~ is sharply raised — **respiratory acidosis**; HCO~3~^−^ is also raised and pH is almost normal — this is **chronic (compensated)** respiratory acidosis with **renal compensation**: the kidneys have increased the excretion of H^+^ and NH~4~^+^ and retained HCO~3~^−^. Check: pH = 6.1 + lg(33 / 1.8) ≈ 7.36. In such patients breathing is driven more by hypoxia; if a lot of oxygen is given, ventilation may weaken, pCO~2~ may rise further and the acidosis may deepen. Therefore controlled oxygen is given to keep SaO~2~ at 88–92 %.
